questions.explanation_text: (A) The stability of a complex increases when the ligand is stronger (i.e., stronger field/stronger bonding ligand gives more stable complex). The ligand strength order given is: $SCN^{-}<OH^{-}<C_{2}OH_{4}^{-2}$ Also, $C_{2}O_{4}^{-2}$ (oxalate) is a bidentate ligand. Because of the chelate effect , complexes with bidentate ligands are generally more stable. So, $[Fe(C_{2}O_{4})_{3}]^{3-}$ is the most stable among the given complexes. Hence, statement (A) is true. (B) en (ethylenediamine) is also a chelating (bidentate) ligand, while $NH_{3}$ is monodentate (non-chelating). Due to the chelate effect, $[Cu(en)_{2}]^{2+}$ is more stable than $[Cu(NH_{3})_{4}]^{2+}$ . So, statement (B) is false. $\begin{aligned} (c) & [Fe(CN)_{6}]^{-4} \\ & Fe^{+2}=4s^{\circ}\text{3d}^{6} \end{aligned}$ $CN^{-}=$ strong field ligand, so it forms a low spin complex. Because $CN^{-}$ is a strong field ligand, electrons pair up in the $3d$ orbitals. This leads to an inner orbital complex with $d^{2}sp^{3}$ hybridisation for Fe. So, statement (C) is true. (D) $[Fe(NO_{2})_{3}Cl_{3}]^{-2}$ and $[Fe(0NO)_{3}Cl_{3}]^{-2}$ Linkage isomerism is shown when an ambidentate ligand can donate electrons through two different atoms. Here, $NO_{2}^{-}$ can coordinate through N (nitro) or through O (nitrito). Therefore, the complex shows linkage isomerism. So, statement (D) is true. (E) $NO_{2}^{-}$ and $SCN^{-}$ are ambidentate ligands (they can attach through different atoms). $S$ -donor $\le ftarrow S=C=N^{\circ} \rightarrow N$ -donor So, the statement “ $NO_{2}^{-}$ and $SCN^{-}$ ligands are NOT ambidentate ligands” is incorrect. Hence, statement (E) is false.
questions.explanation_html:
(A) The stability of a complex increases when the ligand is stronger (i.e., stronger field/stronger bonding ligand gives more stable complex).

The ligand strength order given is:

$SCN^{-}<OH^{-}<C_{2}OH_{4}^{-2}$

Also, $C_{2}O_{4}^{-2}$ (oxalate) is a bidentate ligand. Because of the chelate effect, complexes with bidentate ligands are generally more stable.

So, $[Fe(C_{2}O_{4})_{3}]^{3-}$ is the most stable among the given complexes. Hence, statement (A) is true.

(B) en (ethylenediamine) is also a chelating (bidentate) ligand, while $NH_{3}$ is monodentate (non-chelating).

Due to the chelate effect, $[Cu(en)_{2}]^{2+}$ is more stable than $[Cu(NH_{3})_{4}]^{2+}$ .

So, statement (B) is false.

$\begin{aligned} (c) & [Fe(CN)_{6}]^{-4} \\ & Fe^{+2}=4s^{\circ}\text{3d}^{6} \end{aligned}$

        $CN^{-}=$ strong field ligand, so it forms a low spin complex.

Because $CN^{-}$ is a strong field ligand, electrons pair up in the $3d$ orbitals. This leads to an inner orbital complex with $d^{2}sp^{3}$ hybridisation for Fe.

So, statement (C) is true.

(D) $[Fe(NO_{2})_{3}Cl_{3}]^{-2}$ and $[Fe(0NO)_{3}Cl_{3}]^{-2}$

Linkage isomerism is shown when an ambidentate ligand can donate electrons through two different atoms.

Here, $NO_{2}^{-}$ can coordinate through N (nitro) or through O (nitrito). Therefore, the complex shows linkage isomerism.

So, statement (D) is true.

(E) $NO_{2}^{-}$ and $SCN^{-}$ are ambidentate ligands (they can attach through different atoms).

$S$ -donor $\le ftarrow S=C=N^{\circ} \rightarrow N$ -donor

So, the statement “ $NO_{2}^{-}$ and $SCN^{-}$ ligands are NOT ambidentate ligands” is incorrect.

Hence, statement (E) is false.

Since $H_{2}O$ is a weak field ligand, all these octahedral complexes will be high spin. Now find oxidation state, electronic configuration, number of unpaired electrons, and then magnetic moment. A. $[Cr(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+}$ Here, chromium is in $+2$ oxidation state. Atomic number of Cr = $24$ Neutral Cr: $Cr=[Ar]3d^{5}4s^{1}$ So, $Cr^{2+}=3d^{4}$ For high spin $d^{4}$ , number of unpaired electrons: $n=4$ Thus, $\mu=\sqrt{4(4+2)}=\sqrt{24} \approx 4.90\text{BM}$ So, A $\rightarrow$ III B. $[Co(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+}$ Cobalt is in $+2$ oxidation state. Atomic number of Cu = $29$ $Cu^{2+}=3d^{9}$ For $d^{9}$ , number of unpaired electrons: $n=1$ Thus, $\mu=\sqrt{1(1+2)}=\sqrt{3} \approx 1.73\text{BM}$ So, C $\rightarrow$ IV D. $[Mn(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+}$ Manganese is in $+2$ oxidation state. Atomic number of Mn = $25$ $Mn^{2+}=3d^{5}$ For high spin $d^{5}$ , number of unpaired electrons: $n=5$ Thus, $\mu=\sqrt{5(5+2)}=\sqrt{35} \approx 5.92\text{BM}$ So, D $\rightarrow$ II Final matching $\text{A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II}$ So the correct option is: $\text{Option D}$
questions.explanation_html:
For matching, we use the spin-only magnetic moment formula:

$\mu=\sqrt{n(n+2)}\text{BM}$

where $n$ = number of unpaired electrons.

Since $H_{2}O$ is a weak field ligand, all these octahedral complexes will be high spin.

Now find oxidation state, electronic configuration, number of unpaired electrons, and then magnetic moment.

A. $[Cr(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+}$

Here, chromium is in $+2$ oxidation state.

Atomic number of Cr = $24$

Neutral Cr:

$Cr=[Ar]3d^{5}4s^{1}$

So,

$Cr^{2+}=3d^{4}$

For high spin $d^{4}$ , number of unpaired electrons:

$n=4$

Thus,

$\mu=\sqrt{4(4+2)}=\sqrt{24} \approx 4.90\text{BM}$

So, A $\rightarrow$ III

B. $[Co(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+}$

Cobalt is in $+2$ oxidation state.

Atomic number of Co = $27$

$Co^{2+}=3d^{7}$

For high spin $d^{7}$ , number of unpaired electrons:

$n=3$

Thus,

$\mu=\sqrt{3(3+2)}=\sqrt{15} \approx 3.87\text{BM}$

So, B $\rightarrow$ I

C. $[Cu(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+}$

Copper is in $+2$ oxidation state.

Atomic number of Cu = $29$

$Cu^{2+}=3d^{9}$

For $d^{9}$ , number of unpaired electrons:

$n=1$

Thus,

$\mu=\sqrt{1(1+2)}=\sqrt{3} \approx 1.73\text{BM}$

So, C $\rightarrow$ IV

D. $[Mn(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+}$

Manganese is in $+2$ oxidation state.

Atomic number of Mn = $25$

$Mn^{2+}=3d^{5}$

For high spin $d^{5}$ , number of unpaired electrons:

$n=5$

Thus,

$\mu=\sqrt{5(5+2)}=\sqrt{35} \approx 5.92\text{BM}$

So, D $\rightarrow$ II

Final matching

$\text{A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II}$

So the correct option is:

$\text{Option D}$

questions.explanation_text: Paramagnetic species are those which have one or more unpaired electrons. Let us check each species one by one. 1. In $[CoF_{6}]^{3-}$ , oxidation state of Co is $+3$ (because $6 \times (-1)=-6$ and overall charge is $-3$ ). So Co is $Co^{3+}$ i.e. $d^{6}$ . Since $F^{-}$ is a weak field ligand, it forms a high spin octahedral complex, so unpaired electrons are present. Hence, $[CoF_{6}]^{3-}$ is paramagnetic . 2. In $[TiF_{6}]^{3-}$ , oxidation state of Ti is $+3$ . So Ti is $Ti^{3+}$ i.e. $d^{1}$ . One electron will remain unpaired, so it is paramagnetic . 3. In $[Fe(CN)_{6}]^{3-}$ , oxidation state of Fe is $+3$ . So Fe is $Fe^{3+}$ i.e. $d^{5}$ . Since $CN^{-}$ is a strong field ligand, it gives a low spin octahedral complex, so only one electron remains unpaired. Hence, it is paramagnetic . 4. In $V_{2}O_{5}$ , V is in $+5$ oxidation state, so it is $V^{5+}$ i.e. $d^{0}$ . There are no $d$ -electrons, so there cannot be any unpaired electron. Hence, $V_{2}O_{5}$ is diamagnetic . So, the paramagnetic species are : $[CoF_{6}]^{3-},[TiF_{6}]^{3-},[Fe(CN)_{6}]^{3-}$ And the diamagnetic species is : $V_{2}O_{5}$ Now, compare the complexes in Statement II by counting unpaired electrons. In $K_{4}[Fe(CN)_{6}] \Rightarrow$ Fe is $+2$ (because complex anion is $4-$ ), so $Fe^{2+}$ is $d^{6}$ . With $CN^{-}$ (strong field), it is low spin, so all electrons pair up. Therefore, No. of unpaired electron $=0$ $K_{3}[Fe(CN)_{6}] \Rightarrow$ Fe is $+3$ (complex anion is $3-$ ), so $Fe^{3+}$ is $d^{5}$ . With $CN^{-}$ (strong field), it is low spin, so No. of unpaired electron $=1$ $[Fe(H_{2}O)_{6}]SO_{4} \cdot H_{2}O \Rightarrow$ Here the cation is $[Fe(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+}$ , so Fe is $+2$ i.e. $d^{6}$ . Since $H_{2}O$ is a weak field ligand, it is high spin, so No. of unpaired electron $=4$ $[Fe(H_{2}O)_{6}]Cl_{3} \Rightarrow$ Here the cation is $[Fe(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{3+}$ , so Fe is $+3$ i.e. $d^{5}$ . With $H_{2}O$ (weak field), it is high spin, so No. of unpaired electron $=5$

Paramagnetic species are those which have one or more unpaired electrons.

Let us check each species one by one.

1. In $[CoF_{6}]^{3-}$ , oxidation state of Co is $+3$ (because $6 \times (-1)=-6$ and overall charge is $-3$ ). So Co is $Co^{3+}$ i.e. $d^{6}$ . Since $F^{-}$ is a weak field ligand, it forms a high spin octahedral complex, so unpaired electrons are present. Hence, $[CoF_{6}]^{3-}$ is paramagnetic.

2. In $[TiF_{6}]^{3-}$ , oxidation state of Ti is $+3$ . So Ti is $Ti^{3+}$ i.e. $d^{1}$ . One electron will remain unpaired, so it is paramagnetic.

3. In $[Fe(CN)_{6}]^{3-}$ , oxidation state of Fe is $+3$ . So Fe is $Fe^{3+}$ i.e. $d^{5}$ . Since $CN^{-}$ is a strong field ligand, it gives a low spin octahedral complex, so only one electron remains unpaired. Hence, it is paramagnetic.

4. In $V_{2}O_{5}$ , V is in $+5$ oxidation state, so it is $V^{5+}$ i.e. $d^{0}$ . There are no $d$ -electrons, so there cannot be any unpaired electron. Hence, $V_{2}O_{5}$ is diamagnetic.

So, the paramagnetic species are :

$[CoF_{6}]^{3-},[TiF_{6}]^{3-},[Fe(CN)_{6}]^{3-}$

And the diamagnetic species is : $V_{2}O_{5}$

Now, compare the complexes in Statement II by counting unpaired electrons.

In $K_{4}[Fe(CN)_{6}] \Rightarrow$ Fe is $+2$ (because complex anion is $4-$ ), so $Fe^{2+}$ is $d^{6}$ . With $CN^{-}$ (strong field), it is low spin, so all electrons pair up. Therefore, No. of unpaired electron $=0$

$K_{3}[Fe(CN)_{6}] \Rightarrow$ Fe is $+3$ (complex anion is $3-$ ), so $Fe^{3+}$ is $d^{5}$ . With $CN^{-}$ (strong field), it is low spin, so No. of unpaired electron $=1$

$[Fe(H_{2}O)_{6}]SO_{4} \cdot H_{2}O \Rightarrow$ Here the cation is $[Fe(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+}$ , so Fe is $+2$ i.e. $d^{6}$ . Since $H_{2}O$ is a weak field ligand, it is high spin, so No. of unpaired electron $=4$

$[Fe(H_{2}O)_{6}]Cl_{3} \Rightarrow$ Here the cation is $[Fe(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{3+}$ , so Fe is $+3$ i.e. $d^{5}$ . With $H_{2}O$ (weak field), it is high spin, so No. of unpaired electron $=5$

questions.explanation_text: Statement I (True): The strength of a ligand means how strong it can split the d-orbitals of the metal ion. Among $Cl^{-}$ and $Br^{-}$ , chloride ( $Cl^{-}$ ) is a stronger ligand than bromide ( $Br^{-}$ ). This means for $[CoCl_{4}]^{2-}$ , the energy gap between the two sets of d-orbitals ( $\Delta_{t}$ ) will be larger than in $[CoBr_{4}]^{2-}$ . So, $[CoCl_{4}]^{2-}$ absorbs light of higher energy, and $[CoBr_{4}]^{2-}$ absorbs light of lower energy. $\begin{aligned} & \Delta_{t}:[CoCl_{4}]^{2-}>[CoBr_{4}]^{2-} \\ & \text{Energy absorbed}:[CoCl_{4}]^{2-}>[CoBr_{4}]^{2-} \end{aligned}$ Statement II (False): Here, we compare $I^{-}$ and $Cl^{-}$ as ligands. Iodide ( $I^{-}$ ) is a weaker ligand than chloride ( $Cl^{-}$ ). This means that in $[CoI_{4}]^{2-}$ , the energy difference between the two sets of d-orbitals ( $\Delta_{t}$ ) is smaller than in $[CoCl_{4}]^{2-}$ . $\Delta_{t}:[CoI_{4}]^{2-}<[CoCl_{4}]^{2-}$

The strength of a ligand means how strong it can split the d-orbitals of the metal ion.

Among $Cl^{-}$ and $Br^{-}$ , chloride ( $Cl^{-}$ ) is a stronger ligand than bromide ( $Br^{-}$ ).

This means for $[CoCl_{4}]^{2-}$ , the energy gap between the two sets of d-orbitals ( $\Delta_{t}$ ) will be larger than in $[CoBr_{4}]^{2-}$ .

So, $[CoCl_{4}]^{2-}$ absorbs light of higher energy, and $[CoBr_{4}]^{2-}$ absorbs light of lower energy.

$\begin{aligned} & \Delta_{t}:[CoCl_{4}]^{2-}>[CoBr_{4}]^{2-} \\ & \text{Energy absorbed}:[CoCl_{4}]^{2-}>[CoBr_{4}]^{2-} \end{aligned}$

Statement II (False):

Here, we compare $I^{-}$ and $Cl^{-}$ as ligands. Iodide ( $I^{-}$ ) is a weaker ligand than chloride ( $Cl^{-}$ ).

This means that in $[CoI_{4}]^{2-}$ , the energy difference between the two sets of d-orbitals ( $\Delta_{t}$ ) is smaller than in $[CoCl_{4}]^{2-}$ .

$\Delta_{t}:[CoI_{4}]^{2-}<[CoCl_{4}]^{2-}$

questions.explanation_text: In metal carbonyls, bonding between the metal and CO ligand is explained by synergic bonding . Statement A The metal-carbon bond in metal carbonyls has both $\sigma$ and $\pi$ character. This is correct . CO donates a lone pair from carbon to the metal, forming a $\sigma$ bond. The metal donates electron density back to CO into its vacant $\pi^{∗}$ orbital, forming a $\pi$ bond. So, the bond has both $\sigma$ and $\pi$ character . Statement B Due to synergic bonding interactions between metal and CO ligand, the metal-carbon bond becomes weak. This is incorrect . Synergic bonding actually strengthens the metal-carbon bond because: CO donates electrons to metal by $\sigma$ donation. Metal donates electrons back to CO by $\pi$ back bonding. These two processes reinforce each other, so the M–C bond becomes stronger , not weaker. Statement C The metal-carbon $\sigma$ bond is formed by donation of lone pair of electrons on the carbonyl carbon into a vacant orbital of metal. This is correct . This is exactly the $\sigma$ donation from CO to the metal. Statement D The metal-carbon $\pi$ bond is formed by donation of electrons from filled $d$ -orbital of metal into vacant $\pi^{∗}$ orbital of CO. This is correct . This is called $\pi$ back bonding or back donation . So the correct statements are: $A,C,\text{and}D$ Hence, the correct answer is: $\text{Option B}$
questions.explanation_html:
In metal carbonyls, bonding between the metal and CO ligand is explained by synergic bonding.

Statement A

The metal-carbon bond in metal carbonyls has both $\sigma$ and $\pi$ character.

This is correct.

  • CO donates a lone pair from carbon to the metal, forming a $\sigma$ bond.

  • The metal donates electron density back to CO into its vacant $\pi^{∗}$ orbital, forming a $\pi$ bond.

So, the bond has both $\sigma$ and $\pi$ character.

Statement B

Due to synergic bonding interactions between metal and CO ligand, the metal-carbon bond becomes weak.

This is incorrect.

Synergic bonding actually strengthens the metal-carbon bond because:

  • CO donates electrons to metal by $\sigma$ donation.

  • Metal donates electrons back to CO by $\pi$ back bonding.

These two processes reinforce each other, so the M–C bond becomes stronger, not weaker.

Statement C

The metal-carbon $\sigma$ bond is formed by donation of lone pair of electrons on the carbonyl carbon into a vacant orbital of metal.

This is correct.

This is exactly the $\sigma$ donation from CO to the metal.

Statement D

The metal-carbon $\pi$ bond is formed by donation of electrons from filled $d$ -orbital of metal into vacant $\pi^{∗}$ orbital of CO.

This is correct.

This is called $\pi$ back bonding or back donation.

So the correct statements are:

$A,C,\text{and}D$

Hence, the correct answer is:

$\text{Option B}$

Removing this one electron gives $Sc^{3+}:[Ar]$ , which is a noble gas configuration , hence this removal is comparatively easier. So, third ionization enthalpy is lowest for Sc . Final Answer $\text{Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true}$
questions.explanation_html:
Statement I

We need to compare the energy required to remove the third valence electron, that is, the third ionization enthalpy.

First write the electronic configurations:

  • $Zn:[Ar]3d^{10}4s^{2}$

  • $Mn:[Ar]3d^{5}4s^{2}$

  • $Sc:[Ar]3d^{1}4s^{2}$

  • $Cu:[Ar]3d^{10}4s^{1}$

Now, after removal of two electrons:

  • $Zn^{2+}:[Ar]3d^{10}$

  • $Mn^{2+}:[Ar]3d^{5}$

  • $Sc^{2+}:[Ar]3d^{1}$

  • $Cu^{2+}:[Ar]3d^{9}$

The third electron is now removed from these ions.

Which one will have highest third ionization enthalpy?

For $Zn^{2+}$ , the configuration is $3d^{10}$ , which is a completely filled and very stable configuration. Removing one electron from this is difficult.

So, third ionization enthalpy is highest for Zn.

Which one will have lowest third ionization enthalpy?

For $Sc^{2+}$ , configuration is $3d^{1}$ . Removing this one electron gives $Sc^{3+}:[Ar]$ , which is a noble gas configuration, hence this removal is comparatively easier.

So, third ionization enthalpy is lowest for Sc.

Therefore, Statement I is true.

Statement II

We need the order of complexes in terms of CFSE.

Given complexes:

  1. $[\text{Co(H}_{2}\text{O})_{6}]^{2+}$

  2. $[\text{Co(H}_{2}\text{O})_{6}]^{3+}$

  3. $[\text{Co(en)}_{3}]^{3+}$

Step 1: Find oxidation state and $d$ -configuration

  • In $[\text{Co(H}_{2}\text{O})_{6}]^{2+}$ , cobalt is $Co^{2+}$

    $Co:[Ar]3d^{7}4s^{2}$

    $Co^{2+}:3d^{7}$

  • In $[\text{Co(H}_{2}\text{O})_{6}]^{3+}$ , cobalt is $Co^{3+}$

    $Co^{3+}:3d^{6}$

  • In $[\text{Co(en)}_{3}]^{3+}$ , cobalt is also $Co^{3+}$

    so it is also $3d^{6}$

Step 2: Nature of ligand and spin state

  • $H_{2}O$ is a weak field ligand

  • $en$ is a stronger field ligand than $H_{2}O$

So:

  • $[\text{Co(H}_{2}\text{O})_{6}]^{2+}$ is octahedral, weak field, $d^{7}$

    generally high spin

  • $[\text{Co(H}_{2}\text{O})_{6}]^{3+}$ is octahedral, $d^{6}$

    because of higher charge on $Co^{3+}$ , splitting is larger; this complex is effectively low spin

  • $[\text{Co(en)}_{3}]^{3+}$ is octahedral, $d^{6}$ , strong field

    definitely low spin

Step 3: Calculate CFSE

1. $[\text{Co(H}_{2}\text{O})_{6}]^{2+}$ : high-spin $d^{7}$

Configuration: $t_{2g}^{5}e_{g}^{2}$

$CFSE=5(-0.4\Delta_{o})+2(+0.6\Delta_{o})=-2.0\Delta_{o}+1.2\Delta_{o}=-0.8\Delta_{o}$

Magnitude of CFSE $=0.8\Delta_{o}$

2. $[\text{Co(H}_{2}\text{O})_{6}]^{3+}$ : low-spin $d^{6}$

Configuration: $t_{2g}^{6}e_{g}^{0}$

$CFSE=6(-0.4\Delta_{o})=-2.4\Delta_{o}$

Magnitude $=2.4\Delta_{o}$

3. $[\text{Co(en)}_{3}]^{3+}$ : low-spin $d^{6}$

Also $t_{2g}^{6}e_{g}^{0}$ , so

$CFSE=-2.4\Delta_{o}$

But here $en$ is stronger field than $H_{2}O$ , so $\Delta_{o}$ is larger.

Hence CFSE magnitude is greater for $[\text{Co(en)}_{3}]^{3+}$ than for $[\text{Co(H}_{2}\text{O})_{6}]^{3+}$ .

So the order is:

$[\text{Co(H}_{2}\text{O})_{6}]^{2+}<[\text{Co(H}_{2}\text{O})_{6}]^{3+}<[\text{Co(en)}_{3}]^{3+}$

Therefore, Statement II is also true.

Final Answer

$\text{Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true}$

questions.explanation_text: Option D is correct. 1) $Ni(CO)_{4}$ Oxidation state of Ni: CO is a neutral ligand, so Ni is in $0$ state. Electronic configuration: $Ni(0) \Rightarrow 3d^{10}4s^{0}$ Since it is $d^{10}$ , all electrons are paired. Hence, $Ni(CO)_{4}$ is diamagnetic . 2) $[Ni(CN)_{4}]^{2-}$ Oxidation state of Ni: $x+4(-1)=-2 \Rightarrow x=+2$ So, $Ni^{2+}$ is $3d^{8}$ . $CN^{-}$ is a strong field ligand , causes pairing of electrons. For $Ni^{2+}(d^{8})$ with strong field ligands, complex becomes square planar (inner orbital), and all electrons get paired. Hence, $[Ni(CN)_{4}]^{2-}$ is diamagnetic . 3) $[NiCl_{4}]^{2-}$ Oxidation state of Ni: $x+4(-1)=-2 \Rightarrow x=+2$ So, again $Ni^{2+}$ is $3d^{8}$ . $Cl^{-}$ is a weak field ligand , so it does not cause pairing. Such complexes are generally tetrahedral (outer orbital) and remain high spin , leaving 2 unpaired electrons . Hence, $[NiCl_{4}]^{2-}$ is paramagnetic . Therefore: $Ni(CO)_{4}$ → diamagnetic $[Ni(CN)_{4}]^{2-}$ → diamagnetic $[NiCl_{4}]^{2-}$ → paramagnetic So, the correct statement is Option D .
questions.explanation_html:
Option D is correct.

1) $Ni(CO)_{4}$

  • Oxidation state of Ni: CO is a neutral ligand, so Ni is in $0$ state.

  • Electronic configuration: $Ni(0) \Rightarrow 3d^{10}4s^{0}$

  • Since it is $d^{10}$ , all electrons are paired.

  • Hence, $Ni(CO)_{4}$ is diamagnetic.

2) $[Ni(CN)_{4}]^{2-}$

  • Oxidation state of Ni:

    $x+4(-1)=-2 \Rightarrow x=+2$

  • So, $Ni^{2+}$ is $3d^{8}$ .

  • $CN^{-}$ is a strong field ligand, causes pairing of electrons.

  • For $Ni^{2+}(d^{8})$ with strong field ligands, complex becomes square planar (inner orbital), and all electrons get paired.

  • Hence, $[Ni(CN)_{4}]^{2-}$ is diamagnetic.

3) $[NiCl_{4}]^{2-}$

  • Oxidation state of Ni:

    $x+4(-1)=-2 \Rightarrow x=+2$

  • So, again $Ni^{2+}$ is $3d^{8}$ .

  • $Cl^{-}$ is a weak field ligand, so it does not cause pairing.

  • Such complexes are generally tetrahedral (outer orbital) and remain high spin, leaving 2 unpaired electrons.

  • Hence, $[NiCl_{4}]^{2-}$ is paramagnetic.

Therefore:

  • $Ni(CO)_{4}$ → diamagnetic

  • $[Ni(CN)_{4}]^{2-}$ → diamagnetic

  • $[NiCl_{4}]^{2-}$ → paramagnetic

So, the correct statement is Option D.

questions.explanation_html:
For coordination compounds, only the ions outside the coordination sphere dissociate in water and give precipitates.

1) Identify free ions in solution

(i) $[Co(NH_{3})_{5}SO_{4}]Br$

Here $Br^{-}$ is outside the bracket, so in water:

$[Co(NH_{3})_{5}SO_{4}]Br \rightarrow [Co(NH_{3})_{5}SO_{4}]^{+}+Br^{-}$

So it gives $1$ mol $Br^{-}$ per mol of salt.

(ii) $[Co(NH_{3})_{5}Br]SO_{4}$

Here $SO_{4}^{2-}$ is outside the bracket, so:

$[Co(NH_{3})_{5}Br]SO_{4} \rightarrow [Co(NH_{3})_{5}Br]^{2+}+SO_{4}^{2-}$

So it gives $1$ mol $SO_{4}^{2-}$ per mol of salt.

2) Moles present in 2 L of mixture X

Total solution volume $=4L$ , and we take $2L$ , i.e. half.

So in $2L$ :

  • From $0.4$ mol of $[Co(NH_{3})_{5}SO_{4}]Br$ , we have $0.2$ mol of this salt $\Rightarrow 0.2$ mol $Br^{-}$ .

  • From $0.4$ mol of $[Co(NH_{3})_{5}Br]SO_{4}$ , we have $0.2$ mol of this salt $\Rightarrow 0.2$ mol $SO_{4}^{2-}$ .

3) Precipitates formed

With excess $AgNO_{3}$ (in 2 L):

$Ag^{+}$ precipitates $Br^{-}$ as $AgBr$ :

$Ag^{+}+Br^{-} \rightarrow AgBr(s)$

So moles of precipitate $Y=0.2$ mol (as $AgBr$ ).

With excess $BaCl_{2}$ (in remaining 2 L):

$Ba^{2+}$ precipitates $SO_{4}^{2-}$ as $BaSO_{4}$ :

$Ba^{2+}+SO_{4}^{2-} \rightarrow BaSO_{4}(s)$

So moles of precipitate $Z=0.2$ mol (as $BaSO_{4}$ ).

Correct option

$\text{Option C:}0.2\text{mol of}Z\text{is formed.}$

(Also, $Y=AgBr$ and $Z=BaSO_{4}$ .)

questions.explanation_html:
For $[Ni(PPh_{3})_{2}Cl_{2}]$ :

1) Oxidation state and $d$ -electron count

$PPh_{3}$ is neutral and each $Cl$ is $-1$ .

So oxidation state of Ni is $+2$ .

$Ni^{2+} \Rightarrow 3d^{8}$

2) Geometry using given information (paramagnetic)

For $Ni^{2+}$ ( $d^{8}$ ):

  • Square planar complexes are usually diamagnetic (all electrons paired).

  • Since the complex is paramagnetic, it must be tetrahedral (in NCERT level treatment).

So geometry is tetrahedral and it has 2 unpaired electrons.

Check each statement

A. The complex exhibits geometrical isomerism.

In a tetrahedral complex, all four positions are equivalent, so an $MA_{2}B_{2}$ type complex does not show cis–trans isomerism.

So A is incorrect.

B. The complex is white in colour.

Tetrahedral $Ni^{2+}$ complexes are generally coloured due to $d$ – $d$ transitions; “white” is not expected.

So B is incorrect.

C. Spin-only magnetic moment is $2.84BM$ .

Number of unpaired electrons $n=2$ .

$\mu_{\text{so}}=\sqrt{n(n+2)}=\sqrt{2(2+2)}=\sqrt{8}=2.83BM \approx 2.84BM$

So C is correct.

D. CFSE is $-0.8\Delta_{o}$ .

For tetrahedral splitting, we must use $\Delta_{t}$ , not $\Delta_{o}$ .

For $d^{8}$ tetrahedral: $e^{4}t_{2}^{4}$

$\text{CFSE}=4(-0.6\Delta_{t})+4(+0.4\Delta_{t})=(-2.4+1.6)\Delta_{t}=-0.8\Delta_{t}$

So writing $-0.8\Delta_{o}$ is wrong.

So D is incorrect.

E. Geometry similar to $Ni(CO)_{4}$ .

$Ni(CO)_{4}$ is tetrahedral, and this complex is also tetrahedral (as concluded from paramagnetism).

So E is correct.

Incorrect statements: A, B and D

✅ Correct option: Option B (A, B and D Only)

questions.explanation_text: Let the compound be of the type $[\text{Cr}(\text{H}_{2}\text{O})_{x}\text{Cl}_{y}]\text{Cl}_{3-y} \cdot n\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ Since it is a $1:3$ electrolyte, it gives a total of $4$ ions in solution. So, the complex must be: $[\text{Cr}(\text{H}_{2}\text{O})_{6}]\text{Cl}_{3}$ because this dissociates as $[\text{Cr}(\text{H}_{2}\text{O})_{6}]^{3+}+3\text{Cl}^{-}$ Now calculate moles of the complex. Molar mass of $\text{CrCl}_{3} \cdot 6\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ : $=52+3(35.5)+6(18)$ $=52+106.5+108=266.5\text{g mol}^{-1}$ Moles of complex taken: $\frac{5.33}{266.5}=0.02\text{mol}$ Now, mass of AgCl formed $=8.61\text{g}$ Molar mass of AgCl: $108+35.5=143.5\text{g mol}^{-1}$ Moles of AgCl formed: $\frac{8.61}{143.5}=0.06\text{mol}$ Required ratio: $\frac{\text{moles of complex reacted}}{\text{moles of AgCl formed}}=\frac{0.02}{0.06}=\frac{1}{3}=0.3333$ Now express this as $x \times 10^{-2}$ So, $0.3333=33.33 \times 10^{-2}$ Nearest integer $=33$ . Final answer: $33$
questions.explanation_html:
Let the compound be of the type

$[\text{Cr}(\text{H}_{2}\text{O})_{x}\text{Cl}_{y}]\text{Cl}_{3-y} \cdot n\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$

Since it is a $1:3$ electrolyte, it gives a total of $4$ ions in solution.

So, the complex must be:

$[\text{Cr}(\text{H}_{2}\text{O})_{6}]\text{Cl}_{3}$

because this dissociates as

$[\text{Cr}(\text{H}_{2}\text{O})_{6}]^{3+}+3\text{Cl}^{-}$

Now calculate moles of the complex.

Molar mass of $\text{CrCl}_{3} \cdot 6\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ :

$=52+3(35.5)+6(18)$

$=52+106.5+108=266.5\text{g mol}^{-1}$

Moles of complex taken:

$\frac{5.33}{266.5}=0.02\text{mol}$

Now, mass of AgCl formed $=8.61\text{g}$

Molar mass of AgCl:

$108+35.5=143.5\text{g mol}^{-1}$

Moles of AgCl formed:

$\frac{8.61}{143.5}=0.06\text{mol}$

Required ratio:

$\frac{\text{moles of complex reacted}}{\text{moles of AgCl formed}}=\frac{0.02}{0.06}=\frac{1}{3}=0.3333$

Now express this as

$x \times 10^{-2}$

So,

$0.3333=33.33 \times 10^{-2}$

Nearest integer $=33$ .

Final answer:

$33$

questions.explanation_text: $\text{Statement I :}$ In an octahedral field, the five $d$ -orbitals split into two sets: lower-energy $t_{2g}$ and higher-energy $e_{g}$ . Each electron placed in the higher-energy $e_{g}$ orbitals increases (destabilizes) the energy by $+0.6\Delta_{o}$ . Each electron placed in the lower-energy $t_{2g}$ orbitals decreases (stabilizes) the energy by $-0.4\Delta_{o}$ . So, when electrons go into $e_{g}$ , the crystal field stabilisation becomes less (energy goes up), and when electrons go into $t_{2g}$ , the stabilisation becomes more (energy goes down). Statement II : In free atomic state of transition metal, degeneracy of d-orbrital is maintained. In the free (isolated) metal ion, all five $d$ -orbitals have the same energy, so they are degenerate. When ligands approach to form a complex, the metal–ligand interactions are not the same for all $d$ -orbitals. Because of this, the five $d$ -orbitals split into two sets (like $t_{2g}$ and $e_{g}$ in octahedral complexes), and the degeneracy is removed.
questions.explanation_html:
$\text{Statement I :}$

In an octahedral field, the five $d$ -orbitals split into two sets: lower-energy $t_{2g}$ and higher-energy $e_{g}$ .

Each electron placed in the higher-energy $e_{g}$ orbitals increases (destabilizes) the energy by $+0.6\Delta_{o}$ .

Each electron placed in the lower-energy $t_{2g}$ orbitals decreases (stabilizes) the energy by $-0.4\Delta_{o}$ .

So, when electrons go into $e_{g}$ , the crystal field stabilisation becomes less (energy goes up), and when electrons go into $t_{2g}$ , the stabilisation becomes more (energy goes down).

Statement II : In free atomic state of transition metal, degeneracy of d-orbrital is maintained.

In the free (isolated) metal ion, all five $d$ -orbitals have the same energy, so they are degenerate.

When ligands approach to form a complex, the metal–ligand interactions are not the same for all $d$ -orbitals.

Because of this, the five $d$ -orbitals split into two sets (like $t_{2g}$ and $e_{g}$ in octahedral complexes), and the degeneracy is removed.

questions.explanation_text: Coordination Isomerism arises from the interchange of ligands between cationic and anionic entities of different metal ions present in a complex. When the complete interchange of ligands takes place, it must result in a new, chemically distinct isomer. Let us evaluate each of the given choices under this concept: A. $[Ag(NH_{3})_{2}][Ag(CN)_{2}]$ : Both the cationic and anionic entities contain the same metal ion ( $\text{Ag}$ ). If we fully interchange the ligands, we get $[Ag(CN)_{2}]^{-}[Ag(NH_{3})_{2}]^{+}$ , which is exactly the same compound written in reverse order. Further, a partial interchange leads to neutral molecules $[Ag(NH_{3})(CN)]$ , which destroys the cation-anion pair. Hence, it does not show coordination isomerism. B. $[Co(NH_{3})_{6}][Cr(CN)_{6}]$ : This complex contains two different metal ions ( $\text{Co}$ and $\text{Cr}$ ). By interchanging the ligands between the cationic and anionic coordination spheres, we get a completely new distinct complex: $[Cr(NH_{3})_{6}][Co(CN)_{6}]$ . Hence, it shows coordination isomerism. (This is also the classic example mentioned in NCERT). C. $[Co(NH_{3})_{6}][Co(CN)_{6}]$ : Both entities contain the same metal ion ( $\text{Co}$ ). A complete interchange of all ligands gives $[Co(CN)_{6}]^{3-}[Co(NH_{3})_{6}]^{3+}$ , which is exactly the same coordination compound. According to the strict NCERT definition requiring different metal ions for complete interchange, it does not exhibit coordination isomerism. D. $[Fe(NH_{3})_{6}][Co(CN)_{6}]$ : This complex has two different metal ions ( $\text{Fe}$ and $\text{Co}$ ). Exchanging the primary coordination spheres yields a distinct coordination isomer: $[Co(NH_{3})_{6}][Fe(CN)_{6}]$ . Hence, it shows coordination isomerism. E. $[Co(NH_{3})_{6}][Fe(CN)_{6}]$ : This complex is exactly the coordination isomer of the complex described in option D. Since it consists of different metal ions ( $\text{Co}$ and $\text{Fe}$ ), exchanging its ligands will yield the complex in D. Thus, it also shows coordination isomerism. Conclusion: Complexes B, D, and E exhibit coordination isomerism because they possess differently named metal ions in their cationic and anionic parts, allowing the exchange of ligands to produce distinctly new isomers. Correct Answer: Option B (B, D and E Only)

Let us evaluate each of the given choices under this concept:

  • A. $[Ag(NH_{3})_{2}][Ag(CN)_{2}]$ : Both the cationic and anionic entities contain the same metal ion ( $\text{Ag}$ ). If we fully interchange the ligands, we get $[Ag(CN)_{2}]^{-}[Ag(NH_{3})_{2}]^{+}$ , which is exactly the same compound written in reverse order. Further, a partial interchange leads to neutral molecules $[Ag(NH_{3})(CN)]$ , which destroys the cation-anion pair. Hence, it does not show coordination isomerism.

  • B. $[Co(NH_{3})_{6}][Cr(CN)_{6}]$ : This complex contains two different metal ions ( $\text{Co}$ and $\text{Cr}$ ). By interchanging the ligands between the cationic and anionic coordination spheres, we get a completely new distinct complex: $[Cr(NH_{3})_{6}][Co(CN)_{6}]$ . Hence, it shows coordination isomerism. (This is also the classic example mentioned in NCERT).

  • C. $[Co(NH_{3})_{6}][Co(CN)_{6}]$ : Both entities contain the same metal ion ( $\text{Co}$ ). A complete interchange of all ligands gives $[Co(CN)_{6}]^{3-}[Co(NH_{3})_{6}]^{3+}$ , which is exactly the same coordination compound. According to the strict NCERT definition requiring different metal ions for complete interchange, it does not exhibit coordination isomerism.

  • D. $[Fe(NH_{3})_{6}][Co(CN)_{6}]$ : This complex has two different metal ions ( $\text{Fe}$ and $\text{Co}$ ). Exchanging the primary coordination spheres yields a distinct coordination isomer: $[Co(NH_{3})_{6}][Fe(CN)_{6}]$ . Hence, it shows coordination isomerism.

  • E. $[Co(NH_{3})_{6}][Fe(CN)_{6}]$ : This complex is exactly the coordination isomer of the complex described in option D. Since it consists of different metal ions ( $\text{Co}$ and $\text{Fe}$ ), exchanging its ligands will yield the complex in D. Thus, it also shows coordination isomerism.

Conclusion:

Complexes B, D, and E exhibit coordination isomerism because they possess differently named metal ions in their cationic and anionic parts, allowing the exchange of ligands to produce distinctly new isomers.

Correct Answer:

Option B (B, D and E Only)

questions.explanation_text: For each ion, first find its $3d$ electron count after losing electrons to form the $3+$ charge. Since all are low spin octahedral complexes, electrons will first pair up in the lower-energy $t_{2g}$ orbitals before entering the higher-energy $e_{g}$ orbitals. $\begin{aligned} & Co^{3+} \rightarrow 3d^{6} \Rightarrow t_{2g}^{2,2,2}e_{g}^{0,0},\text{unpaired electron}=0 \\ & Fe^{3+} \rightarrow 3d^{5} \Rightarrow t_{2g}^{2,2,1}e_{g}^{0,0}\text{unpaired electron}=1 \\ & Cr^{3+} \rightarrow 3d^{3} \Rightarrow t_{2g}^{1,1,1}e_{g}^{0,0}\text{unpaired electron}=3 \\ & Mn^{3+} \rightarrow 3d^{4} \Rightarrow t_{2g}^{2,1,1}e_{g}^{0,0}\text{unpaired electron}=2 \end{aligned}$ Now compare the number of unpaired electrons: $Cr^{3+}$ has $3$ , $Mn^{3+}$ has $2$ , $Fe^{3+}$ has $1$ , and $Co^{3+}$ has $0$ . So, the decreasing order of unpaired electrons is: $Cr^{3+}>Mn^{3+}>Fe^{3+}>Co^{3+}$

questions.explanation_text: $\begin{aligned} Sc^{+3} & 18 \\ Cr^{+2} & 22 \\ Mn^{+3} & 22 \\ Co^{+3} & 24 \\ Fe^{+3} & 23 \end{aligned}$ In the table, the number written for each ion is its total number of electrons. $Cr^{2+}$ and $Mn^{3+}$ both have $22$ electrons, so they are isoelectronic (same number of electrons). questions.question_html: The crystal field splitting energy of $[Co(\text{oxalate})_{3}]^{3-}$ complex is ' $n^{'}$ times that of the $[Cr(\text{oxalate})_{3}]^{3-}$ complex. Here ' $n$ ' is $____$ . (Assume $\Delta_{0}≫P$ )
questions.explanation_text: Since $\Delta_{0}≫P$ , we ignore pairing energy and decide the electron arrangement mainly using $\Delta_{0}$ . For $[Co(ox)_{3}]^{3-}$ : $Co^{+3}$ has configuration $d^{6}$ . In an octahedral field (given $\Delta_{0}≫P$ ), all 6 electrons occupy $t_{2g}$ first, so the distribution is $t_{2}g^{2,2,2}eg^{0,0}$ . Each electron in $t_{2g}$ gives CFSE of $(-0.4\Delta_{0})$ , so $CFSE=6 \times (-0.4\Delta_{0})=-2.4\Delta_{0}$ For $[Cr(ox_{3})]^{3-}$ : $Cr^{+3}$ has configuration $d^{3}$ . So the electrons occupy $t_{2g}$ as $t_{2}g^{1,1,1}eg^{0,0}$ . Hence, $CFSE=3 \times (-0.4\Delta_{0})=-1.2\Delta_{0}$ Now, $\frac{(CFSE)_{Co^{+3}}}{(CFSE)_{Cr^{+3}}}=\frac{-2.4\Delta_{0}}{-1.2\Delta_{0}}=2$ So, $n=2$ .

questions.explanation_text: Enthalpy of atomisation is the energy needed to break $1$ mole of a metal (in solid state) into its separate atoms (in gaseous state). In transition metals, metallic bonding becomes stronger when there are more unpaired electrons. This is because unpaired electrons can take part more effectively in metal–metal bonding. So, if a transition metal atom has a large number of unpaired electrons, its metallic bonds are stronger, and more energy is required to convert the metal into atoms. Therefore, more unpaired electrons $∝$ stronger metallic bonding $∝$ higher enthalpy of atomisation. Hence, Statement I is correct . $[Fe(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{3+}$ is an octahedral complex (coordination number $6$ ). In an octahedral field, the $d$ -orbitals split as: $d_{xy}=d_{xz}=d_{yz}<d_{x^{2}-y^{2}}=d_{z^{2}}$ $[Ni(Cl)_{4}]^{2-}$ is a tetrahedral complex (coordination number $4$ ). In a tetrahedral field, the splitting is reversed compared to octahedral, i.e.: $d_{x^{2}-y^{2}}=d_{z^{2}}<d_{xy}=d_{xz}=d_{yz}$ So, the given splittings match the correct orbital splitting patterns for these two geometries. Hence, Statement II is also correct .

questions.explanation_text: For all the three complexes, the metal ion is $Ni^{2+}$ . The electronic configuration of Ni is $Ni:[Ar]3d^{8}4s^{2}$ So, $Ni^{2+}:[Ar]3d^{8}$ Now let us examine each complex. 1. Complex $(A)=[Ni(en)_{3}]^{2+}$ Here, $en$ is ethane-1,2-diamine, a neutral bidentate ligand. Coordination number $=6$ Geometry $=$ octahedral For an octahedral $d^{8}$ configuration, the arrangement is: $t_{2g}^{6}e_{g}^{2}$ This gives 2 unpaired electrons . So, for $(A)$ : $\text{Number of unpaired electrons}=2$ 2. Complex $(B)=[NiCl_{4}]^{2-}$ Coordination number $=4$ Since $Cl^{-}$ is a weak ligand, this complex is tetrahedral . For tetrahedral $d^{8}$ , the splitting is small, and the electrons remain high spin. Hence, it has 2 unpaired electrons . So, for $(B)$ : $\text{Number of unpaired electrons}=2$ 3. Complex $(C)=[Ni(NH_{3})_{6}]^{2+}$ Coordination number $=6$ Geometry $=$ octahedral Again, for octahedral $d^{8}$ : $t_{2g}^{6}e_{g}^{2}$ So it also has 2 unpaired electrons . Thus, for $(C)$ : $\text{Number of unpaired electrons}=2$ Frequency of absorption The frequency of absorbed light depends on crystal field splitting: $\Delta∝\nu$ Greater the splitting, greater the frequency of absorption. Now compare ligand strengths: $en>NH_{3}>Cl^{-}$ Also, tetrahedral complexes have smaller splitting than octahedral complexes. So, $[Ni(en)_{3}]^{2+}$ has the highest $\Delta$ $[Ni(NH_{3})_{6}]^{2+}$ has next $[NiCl_{4}]^{2-}$ has the least Therefore, order of frequency of absorption is: $(A)>(C)>(B)$ Hence the correct option is: $\text{Option A}$
questions.explanation_html:
For all the three complexes, the metal ion is $Ni^{2+}$ .

The electronic configuration of Ni is

$Ni:[Ar]3d^{8}4s^{2}$

So,

$Ni^{2+}:[Ar]3d^{8}$

Now let us examine each complex.

1. Complex $(A)=[Ni(en)_{3}]^{2+}$

Here, $en$ is ethane-1,2-diamine, a neutral bidentate ligand.

  • Coordination number $=6$

  • Geometry $=$ octahedral

For an octahedral $d^{8}$ configuration, the arrangement is:

$t_{2g}^{6}e_{g}^{2}$

This gives 2 unpaired electrons.

So, for $(A)$ :

$\text{Number of unpaired electrons}=2$

2. Complex $(B)=[NiCl_{4}]^{2-}$

  • Coordination number $=4$

  • Since $Cl^{-}$ is a weak ligand, this complex is tetrahedral.

For tetrahedral $d^{8}$ , the splitting is small, and the electrons remain high spin.

Hence, it has 2 unpaired electrons.

So, for $(B)$ :

$\text{Number of unpaired electrons}=2$

3. Complex $(C)=[Ni(NH_{3})_{6}]^{2+}$

  • Coordination number $=6$

  • Geometry $=$ octahedral

Again, for octahedral $d^{8}$ :

$t_{2g}^{6}e_{g}^{2}$

So it also has 2 unpaired electrons.

Thus, for $(C)$ :

$\text{Number of unpaired electrons}=2$

Frequency of absorption

The frequency of absorbed light depends on crystal field splitting:

$\Delta∝\nu$

Greater the splitting, greater the frequency of absorption.

Now compare ligand strengths:

$en>NH_{3}>Cl^{-}$

Also, tetrahedral complexes have smaller splitting than octahedral complexes.

So,

  • $[Ni(en)_{3}]^{2+}$ has the highest $\Delta$

  • $[Ni(NH_{3})_{6}]^{2+}$ has next

  • $[NiCl_{4}]^{2-}$ has the least

Therefore, order of frequency of absorption is:

$(A)>(C)>(B)$

Hence the correct option is:

$\text{Option A}$

questions.explanation_text: To decide hybridisation, geometry and magnetic moment, we mainly look at (i) the type of ligands (strong field or weak field) and (ii) the number of unpaired electrons. The spin-only magnetic moment depends on the number of unpaired electrons $n$ . The given results for each complex are summarised below (hybridisation $\Rightarrow$ geometry $\Rightarrow$ number of unpaired electrons $\Rightarrow$ magnetic moment in B.M.). $\begin{aligned} \text{In}K_{3}[Co(CO_{3})_{3}] & \Rightarrow sp^{3}d^{2}\text{hybridized, octahedral} \\ & \Rightarrow 4\text{unpaired electron} \\ & \Rightarrow 4.9\text{B.M.} \\ [Ni(CN)_{4}]^{2-} & \Rightarrow dsp^{2}\text{hybridized, square planar} \\ & \Rightarrow 0\text{unpaired electron} \\ & \Rightarrow 0\text{B.M.} \\ [MnBr_{4}]^{2-} & \Rightarrow sp^{3}\text{hybridized, tetrahedral} \\ & \Rightarrow 5\text{unpaired electron} \\ & \Rightarrow 5.9\text{B.M.} \\ [CoF_{6}]^{2-} & \Rightarrow \text{sp}d^{2}\text{hybridized, octahedral} \\ & \Rightarrow 4\text{unpaired electron} \\ & \Rightarrow 4.9\text{B.M.} \end{aligned}$ So, the hybridisation/geometry and magnetic moments mentioned in the statements match these standard results (based on unpaired electrons in each case).

questions.explanation_text: In this complex, Ni is in the +2 oxidation state (that is, it is present as $Ni^{2+}$ ). A) The nickel dimethylglyoxime complex is a rosy red coloured precipitate, so the statement that it is red in colour is correct. B) This complex is formed (precipitated) in a basic medium (around $pH=9$ ), but it is sparingly soluble in water, not highly soluble. So the statement about high solubility in water at $pH=9$ is incorrect. C) $Ni^{+2}:3d^{8}$ means that $Ni^{2+}$ has 8 electrons in the d-subshell. In this complex, it forms a square planar $dsp^{2}$ complex in which all these electrons get paired. Therefore, the statement that Ni has two unpaired d-electrons is incorrect. Hybridisation : $dsp^{2}$ , which leads to a square planar arrangement of the ligands around the Ni ion. Unpaired $e^{-}=0$ , so the complex is diamagnetic (no unpaired electrons are present). Geometry : Square planar, which is typical for $dsp^{2}$ hybridisation in such $Ni^{2+}$ complexes. D) $N-Ni-N$ Bond angle is close to $90^{\circ}$ in a square planar complex because adjacent bond angles in square planar geometry are approximately $90^{\circ}$ . So statement D is correct. E) Each dimethylglyoxime ligand forms one five-membered chelate ring with the Ni ion. Since there are only two such ligands, 2 five-membered metal-containing rings are formed, not four. So statement E is incorrect.

questions.question_text: A first row transition metal $(M)$ does not liberate $H_{2}$ gas from dilute HCl .1 mol of aqueous solution of $MSO_{4}$ is treated with excess of aqueous KCN and then $H_{2}S(g)$ is passed through the solution. The amount of MS (metal sulphide) formed from the above reaction is $____$ mol.
questions.question_html: A first row transition metal $(M)$ does not liberate $H_{2}$ gas from dilute HCl .1 mol of aqueous solution of $MSO_{4}$ is treated with excess of aqueous KCN and then $H_{2}S(g)$ is passed through the solution. The amount of MS (metal sulphide) formed from the above reaction is $____$ mol.
questions.explanation_text: $Cu\overset{\text{di.}HCl}{\rightarrow \le ftarrow}$ no reaction Step 1: Identify the metal $M$ A first row transition metal that does not liberate $H_{2}$ gas with dilute HCl is $Cu$ (copper). So, $M=Cu$ . Step 2: Reaction of $MSO_{4}$ with excess KCN So $MSO_{4}$ is $CuSO_{4}$ . When $CuSO_{4}$ is treated with excess aqueous KCN, copper forms a very stable (perfect) cyanide complex. $CuSO_{4}\overset{KCN}{\rightarrow \le ftarrow}\underset{\text{perfect complex}}{[Cu(CN)_{4}]^{3-}}\overset{H_{2}S}{\rightarrow \le ftarrow}$ no sulphide ppt Step 3: Passing $H_{2}S$ through the solution Because copper is present as the stable complex $[Cu(CN)_{4}]^{3-}$ , free $Cu^{2+}$ ions are not available in solution. Therefore, $H_{2}S$ cannot precipitate copper sulphide. Final Answer No metal sulphide $MS$ is formed. Hence, the amount of $MS$ formed is $0$ mol.
questions.explanation_html:
$Cu\overset{\text{di.}HCl}{\rightarrow \le ftarrow}$ no reaction

Step 1: Identify the metal $M$

A first row transition metal that does not liberate $H_{2}$ gas with dilute HCl is $Cu$ (copper). So, $M=Cu$ .

Step 2: Reaction of $MSO_{4}$ with excess KCN

So $MSO_{4}$ is $CuSO_{4}$ . When $CuSO_{4}$ is treated with excess aqueous KCN, copper forms a very stable (perfect) cyanide complex.

$CuSO_{4}\overset{KCN}{\rightarrow \le ftarrow}\underset{\text{perfect complex}}{[Cu(CN)_{4}]^{3-}}\overset{H_{2}S}{\rightarrow \le ftarrow}$ no sulphide ppt

Step 3: Passing $H_{2}S$ through the solution

Because copper is present as the stable complex $[Cu(CN)_{4}]^{3-}$ , free $Cu^{2+}$ ions are not available in solution. Therefore, $H_{2}S$ cannot precipitate copper sulphide.

Final Answer

No metal sulphide $MS$ is formed. Hence, the amount of $MS$ formed is $0$ mol.

questions.question_text: X is the number of geometrical isomers exhibited by $[Pt(NH_{3})(H_{2}O)BrCl]$ . Y is the number of optically inactive isomer(s) exhibited by $[CrCl_{2}(ox)_{2}]^{3-}$ Z is the number of geometrical isomers exhibited by $[Co(NH_{3})_{3}(NO_{2})_{3}]$ . The value of $X+Y+Z$ is $____$ .
questions.question_html:
X is the number of geometrical isomers exhibited by $[Pt(NH_{3})(H_{2}O)BrCl]$ .

Y is the number of optically inactive isomer(s) exhibited by $[CrCl_{2}(ox)_{2}]^{3-}$

Z is the number of geometrical isomers exhibited by $[Co(NH_{3})_{3}(NO_{2})_{3}]$ .

The value of $X+Y+Z$ is $____$ .
questions.explanation_text: 1) Find $X$ for $[Pt(NH_{3})(H_{2}O)BrCl]$ Pt in such complexes is usually $Pt(II)$ , which (as per NCERT) forms square planar complexes. The complex is of type $[MABCD]$ (four different ligands). For square planar $[MABCD]$ , the number of geometrical isomers is 3 (based on which ligand is trans to a chosen ligand; distinct trans-pairings give 3 arrangements). So, $X=3.$ 2) Find $Y$ for $[CrCl_{2}(ox)_{2}]^{3-}$ Here $ox$ (oxalate) is a bidentate ligand. Two oxalate ligands occupy $4$ coordination positions, and $2$ positions are occupied by $Cl^{-}$ . So the complex is octahedral of type $[M(AA)_{2}B_{2}]$ . Such complexes show cis–trans isomerism: cis form is optically active (exists as $\Delta$ and $\Lambda$ enantiomers) trans form is optically inactive So optically inactive isomers = only 1 (trans) . Thus, $Y=1.$ 3) Find $Z$ for $[Co(NH_{3})_{3}(NO_{2})_{3}]$ This is an octahedral complex of type $[MA_{3}B_{3}]$ . It shows fac–mer isomerism: fac mer So, $Z=2.$ Final Answer $X+Y+Z=3+1+2=6.$ $6$
questions.explanation_html:
1) Find $X$ for $[Pt(NH_{3})(H_{2}O)BrCl]$

  • Pt in such complexes is usually $Pt(II)$ , which (as per NCERT) forms square planar complexes.

  • The complex is of type $[MABCD]$ (four different ligands).

For square planar $[MABCD]$ , the number of geometrical isomers is 3 (based on which ligand is trans to a chosen ligand; distinct trans-pairings give 3 arrangements).

So, $X=3.$

2) Find $Y$ for $[CrCl_{2}(ox)_{2}]^{3-}$

  • Here $ox$ (oxalate) is a bidentate ligand.

  • Two oxalate ligands occupy $4$ coordination positions, and $2$ positions are occupied by $Cl^{-}$ .

  • So the complex is octahedral of type $[M(AA)_{2}B_{2}]$ .

Such complexes show cis–trans isomerism:

  • cis form is optically active (exists as $\Delta$ and $\Lambda$ enantiomers)

  • trans form is optically inactive

So optically inactive isomers = only 1 (trans).

Thus, $Y=1.$

3) Find $Z$ for $[Co(NH_{3})_{3}(NO_{2})_{3}]$

This is an octahedral complex of type $[MA_{3}B_{3}]$ .

It shows fac–mer isomerism:

  • fac

  • mer

So, $Z=2.$

Final Answer

$X+Y+Z=3+1+2=6.$

$6$

questions.explanation_text: In this octahedral complex with the molecular composition $Co \cdot 5NH_{3} \cdot Cl^{2} \cdot SO_{4}$ , two isomers, A and B, are present. Isomer A is represented as $[Co(NH_{3})_{5}(SO_{4})]Cl$ . When this isomer is dissolved in solution, it reacts with $AgNO_{3}$ , forming a white precipitate of silver chloride ( $AgCl$ ). Isomer B is written as $[Co(NH_{3})_{5}Cl]SO_{4}$ . In solution, it reacts with $BaCl_{2}$ , forming a white precipitate of barium sulfate ( $BaSO_{4}$ ). These two isomers demonstrate ionisation isomerism. This type of isomerism occurs when the exchange of ions inside and outside the coordination sphere of a complex leads to the formation of isomers with different chemical behaviors in solution.

questions.explanation_text: Determine the oxidation state of manganese in $[MnCl_{6}]^{3-}:$ Chloride (Cl⁻) has a charge of -1. With six chloride ions, the total charge contributed by the ligands is $6(-1)=-6.$ Let the oxidation state of Mn be $x.$ Then: $x-6=-3⟹x=+3.$ So, manganese is in the +3 oxidation state. Find the d-electron count for Mn(III): The neutral manganese atom has the electronic configuration $[Ar]3d^{5}4s^{2}.$ Removing three electrons (first from the 4s, then from the 3d) gives: $Mn^{3+}:[Ar]3d^{4}.$ Therefore, Mn(III) is a $d^{4}$ system. Predict the spin state in an octahedral complex: Chloride (Cl⁻) is a weak-field ligand, meaning it produces a relatively small crystal field splitting ( $\Delta_{o}$ ). When $\Delta_{o}$ is small, the pairing energy is higher than $\Delta_{o},$ so electrons prefer to remain unpaired. For a $d^{4}$ configuration in a high-spin octahedral complex, the electrons will be distributed as: Three electrons in the three $t_{2g}$ orbitals (one in each) One electron in one of the $e_{g}$ orbitals This results in a total of 4 unpaired electrons, making the complex paramagnetic. Determine the type of hybridization: In octahedral complexes, the two common hybridizations are: $d^{2}sp^{3}$ (inner orbital complex), typically seen in low-spin complexes where inner 3d orbitals are available because the electrons are paired. $sp^{3}d^{2}$ (outer orbital complex), seen in high-spin complexes where the inner $3d$ orbitals are occupied by unpaired electrons. Since $[MnCl_{6}]^{3-}$ is high-spin (because of Cl⁻ being a weak-field ligand), the inner 3d orbitals are not available for hybridization. Therefore, the complex uses the outer orbitals (the 4s, 4p, and 4d orbitals), leading to an $sp^{3}d^{2}$ hybridization. Conclusion: The hybridization of $[MnCl_{6}]^{3-}$ is $sp^{3}d^{2}.$ It is paramagnetic with four unpaired electrons. Thus, the correct answer is: Option A: $sp^{3}d^{2}$ , paramagnetic with four unpaired electrons.
questions.explanation_html:
Determine the oxidation state of manganese in $[MnCl_{6}]^{3-}:$

Chloride (Cl⁻) has a charge of -1.

With six chloride ions, the total charge contributed by the ligands is $6(-1)=-6.$

Let the oxidation state of Mn be $x.$ Then:

$x-6=-3⟹x=+3.$

So, manganese is in the +3 oxidation state.

Find the d-electron count for Mn(III):

The neutral manganese atom has the electronic configuration $[Ar]3d^{5}4s^{2}.$

Removing three electrons (first from the 4s, then from the 3d) gives:

$Mn^{3+}:[Ar]3d^{4}.$

Therefore, Mn(III) is a $d^{4}$ system.

Predict the spin state in an octahedral complex:

Chloride (Cl⁻) is a weak-field ligand, meaning it produces a relatively small crystal field splitting ( $\Delta_{o}$ ).

When $\Delta_{o}$ is small, the pairing energy is higher than $\Delta_{o},$ so electrons prefer to remain unpaired.

For a $d^{4}$ configuration in a high-spin octahedral complex, the electrons will be distributed as:

Three electrons in the three $t_{2g}$ orbitals (one in each)

One electron in one of the $e_{g}$ orbitals

This results in a total of 4 unpaired electrons, making the complex paramagnetic.

Determine the type of hybridization:

In octahedral complexes, the two common hybridizations are:

$d^{2}sp^{3}$ (inner orbital complex), typically seen in low-spin complexes where inner 3d orbitals are available because the electrons are paired.

$sp^{3}d^{2}$ (outer orbital complex), seen in high-spin complexes where the inner $3d$ orbitals are occupied by unpaired electrons.

Since $[MnCl_{6}]^{3-}$ is high-spin (because of Cl⁻ being a weak-field ligand), the inner 3d orbitals are not available for hybridization.

Therefore, the complex uses the outer orbitals (the 4s, 4p, and 4d orbitals), leading to an $sp^{3}d^{2}$ hybridization.

Conclusion:

The hybridization of $[MnCl_{6}]^{3-}$ is $sp^{3}d^{2}.$

It is paramagnetic with four unpaired electrons.

Thus, the correct answer is:

Option A: $sp^{3}d^{2}$ , paramagnetic with four unpaired electrons.

$x=+3$

$K_{4}[Fe(OH)_{6}]$

$4(+1)+x+6(-1)=0$

$4+x-6=0$

$x=6-4=+2$

Also written as $[Fe(OH)_{6}]^{4-}$

Oxidation state of $Fe \rightarrow +2$

Configuration of $Fe \rightarrow d^{6}s^{2}$

Configuration of $Fe^{+2} \rightarrow d^{6}$

Since OH $^{-}$ is a weak field ligand, no pairing of electrons occurs.

Unpaired electrons = 4

Spin-only magnetic moment

$=\sqrt{n(n+2)}$

$=\sqrt{4(4+2)}$

$=\sqrt{4 \times 6}$

$=\sqrt{24}$

$=4.90$ BM

Spin-only magnetic moments of $K_{3}[Fe(OH)_{6}]$ and $K_{4}[Fe(OH)_{6}]$ respectively are 5.92 and 4.90 B.M.

Correct answer is option (3) 5.92 and 4.90 B.M.

questions.explanation_text: Given the problem, we have the following information: Depression in freezing point, $\Delta T_{f}=0.558^{\circ}\text{C}$ Freezing point depression constant, $k_{f}=1.86\text{K kg mol}^{-1}$ Molal concentration of the solution, $0.1\text{mol kg}^{-1}$ Coordination number of Cr is 6. Using the formula for freezing point depression: $\Delta T_{f}=i \times k_{f} \times m$ where $i$ is the van 't Hoff factor, $k_{f}$ is the freezing point depression constant, and $m$ is the molality of the solution. Substituting the known values: $0.558=i \times 1.86 \times 0.1$ Solving for $i$ : $i=\frac{0.558}{1.86 \times 0.1}=3$ The van 't Hoff factor $i=3$ indicates that the complex ionizes into three particles in solution. Given the coordination number of Cr is 6, we analyze the possible complexes: $[Cr(NH_{3})_{5}Cl]Cl_{2}$ $[Cr(NH_{3})_{4}Cl_{2}]Cl$ $[Cr(NH_{3})_{6}]Cl_{3}$ $[Cr(NH_{3})_{3}Cl_{3}]$ The complex that gives three ions upon dissociation could be $[Cr(NH_{3})_{5}Cl]Cl_{2}$ . This is because the complex will dissociate as: $[Cr(NH_{3})_{5}Cl]^{2+}+2Cl^{-}$ This results in three ions total, matching the van 't Hoff factor $i=3$ . Therefore, the complex is $[Cr(NH_{3})_{5}Cl]Cl_{2}$ .

questions.question_html: The d-orbital electronic configuration of the complex among $[Co(en)_{3}]^{3+},[CoF_{6}]^{3-}$ , $[Mn(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+}$ and $[Zn(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+}$ that has the highest CFSE is :
questions.explanation_text: Identify the oxidation state and d-electron count for each complex: For $[Co(en)_{3}]^{3+}$ : Ethylenediamine (en) is neutral. Oxidation state of cobalt is +3. Cobalt (atomic number 27) in the +3 state gives a $d^{6}$ configuration. With strong/moderate field ligands like en, the complex is low spin, leading to a configuration of $t_{2g}^{6}e_{g}^{0}$ . For $[CoF_{6}]^{3-}$ : Each fluoride ion is $F^{-}$ so, with six of them, Co must be in the +3 state again. However, since fluoride is a weak field ligand, this complex adopts a high spin configuration for $d^{6}$ , resulting in $t_{2g}^{4}e_{g}^{2}$ . For $[Mn(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+}$ : Water is neutral. Manganese in the +2 state gives a $d^{5}$ configuration. With weak field water, the $d^{5}$ configuration is high spin: $t_{2g}^{3}e_{g}^{2}$ . For $[Zn(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+}$ : Zinc in the +2 state has a $d^{10}$ configuration. In an octahedral field, all 10 electrons fill the orbitals as $t_{2g}^{6}e_{g}^{4}$ . Calculate the crystal field stabilization energy (CFSE) for each case: The CFSE in an octahedral field can be estimated as: $CFSE=(n_{t_{2g}} \times -0.4\Delta_{o})+(n_{e_{g}} \times 0.6\Delta_{o})$ For $t_{2g}^{6}e_{g}^{0}$ (low-spin $d^{6}$ in $[Co(en)_{3}]^{3+}$ ): $CFSE=6(-0.4\Delta_{o})+0(0.6\Delta_{o})=-2.4\Delta_{o}$ For $t_{2g}^{4}e_{g}^{2}$ (high-spin $d^{6}$ in $[CoF_{6}]^{3-}$ ): $CFSE=4(-0.4\Delta_{o})+2(0.6\Delta_{o})=-1.6\Delta_{o}+1.2\Delta_{o}=-0.4\Delta_{o}$ For $t_{2g}^{3}e_{g}^{2}$ (high-spin $d^{5}$ in $[Mn(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+}$ ): $CFSE=3(-0.4\Delta_{o})+2(0.6\Delta_{o})=-1.2\Delta_{o}+1.2\Delta_{o}=0$ For $t_{2g}^{6}e_{g}^{4}$ (for $d^{10}$ in $[Zn(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+}$ ): $CFSE=6(-0.4\Delta_{o})+4(0.6\Delta_{o})=-2.4\Delta_{o}+2.4\Delta_{o}=0$ Compare the CFSE values: $t_{2g}^{6}e_{g}^{0}$ gives a CFSE of $-2.4\Delta_{o}$ (most negative, hence highest stabilization). The others result in less stabilization (or net zero). Conclusion: The complex with the highest CFSE is the one with the configuration $t_{2g}^{6}e_{g}^{0}$ , which corresponds to $[Co(en)_{3}]^{3+}$ . Thus, the answer is: Option A: $t_{2g}^{6}e_{g}^{0}$ .

With strong/moderate field ligands like en, the complex is low spin, leading to a configuration of $t_{2g}^{6}e_{g}^{0}$ .

For $[CoF_{6}]^{3-}$ :

Each fluoride ion is $F^{-}$ so, with six of them, Co must be in the +3 state again.

However, since fluoride is a weak field ligand, this complex adopts a high spin configuration for $d^{6}$ , resulting in $t_{2g}^{4}e_{g}^{2}$ .

For $[Mn(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+}$ :

Water is neutral.

Manganese in the +2 state gives a $d^{5}$ configuration.

With weak field water, the $d^{5}$ configuration is high spin: $t_{2g}^{3}e_{g}^{2}$ .

For $[Zn(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+}$ :

Zinc in the +2 state has a $d^{10}$ configuration.

In an octahedral field, all 10 electrons fill the orbitals as $t_{2g}^{6}e_{g}^{4}$ .

Calculate the crystal field stabilization energy (CFSE) for each case:

The CFSE in an octahedral field can be estimated as:

$CFSE=(n_{t_{2g}} \times -0.4\Delta_{o})+(n_{e_{g}} \times 0.6\Delta_{o})$

For $t_{2g}^{6}e_{g}^{0}$ (low-spin $d^{6}$ in $[Co(en)_{3}]^{3+}$ ):

$CFSE=6(-0.4\Delta_{o})+0(0.6\Delta_{o})=-2.4\Delta_{o}$

For $t_{2g}^{4}e_{g}^{2}$ (high-spin $d^{6}$ in $[CoF_{6}]^{3-}$ ):

$CFSE=4(-0.4\Delta_{o})+2(0.6\Delta_{o})=-1.6\Delta_{o}+1.2\Delta_{o}=-0.4\Delta_{o}$

For $t_{2g}^{3}e_{g}^{2}$ (high-spin $d^{5}$ in $[Mn(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+}$ ):

$CFSE=3(-0.4\Delta_{o})+2(0.6\Delta_{o})=-1.2\Delta_{o}+1.2\Delta_{o}=0$

For $t_{2g}^{6}e_{g}^{4}$ (for $d^{10}$ in $[Zn(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+}$ ):

$CFSE=6(-0.4\Delta_{o})+4(0.6\Delta_{o})=-2.4\Delta_{o}+2.4\Delta_{o}=0$

Compare the CFSE values:

$t_{2g}^{6}e_{g}^{0}$ gives a CFSE of $-2.4\Delta_{o}$ (most negative, hence highest stabilization).

The others result in less stabilization (or net zero).

Conclusion:

The complex with the highest CFSE is the one with the configuration $t_{2g}^{6}e_{g}^{0}$ , which corresponds to $[Co(en)_{3}]^{3+}$ .

Thus, the answer is:

Option A: $t_{2g}^{6}e_{g}^{0}$ .

$\Delta_{0}$ value of the octahedral complexes can be calculated using the formula

CASE $=(-0,4\Delta_{0}) \times$ number of electrons in $f_{2g}$ orbitals + $(+0.6\Delta_{0}) \times$ number of electrons in eg orbitals.

The ligand CN $^{-}$ is a strong field ligand and all the complexes form low-spin complex (pairing occurs).

I) $[M_{N}(CN)_{6}]^{3-}$

Oxidation state of $M_{n}:+3$

$Mn$ configuration $\rightarrow d^{5}s^{2}$

$Mn^{+3}$ configuration $\rightarrow d^{4}$

$\begin{aligned} x+6(-1)=-3 \\ x=-3+b=+3 \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} CFSE & =-0.4\Delta_{0} \times 4+(0.6\Delta_{0}) \times 0 \\ & =-1.6\Delta_{0} \end{aligned}$

II) $[Co(CN)_{6}]^{4-}$

Oxidation state of $C_{0}:+2$

$C_{0}$ configuration $\rightarrow d^{7}s^{2}$

$Co^{+2}$ configuration $\rightarrow d^{7}$

$\begin{aligned} \text{CFSE} & =-0.4\Delta_{0} \times 6+(0.6\Delta_{0}) \times 1 \\ & =-2.4\Delta_{0}+0.6\Delta_{0}=-1.8\Delta_{0} \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} x+6(-1) & =-4 \\ x & =-4+6=+2 \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} \text{CFSE} & =-0.4\Delta_{0} \times 6+(0.6\Delta_{10}) \times 1 \\ & =-2.4\Delta_{0}+0.6\Delta_{0}=-1.8\Delta_{0} \end{aligned}$

III) $[Fe(CN)_{6}]^{4-}$

Oxidation state of $Fe:+2$

Fe configuration $\rightarrow d^{6}s^{2}$

$Fe^{+2}$ configuration $\rightarrow d^{6}$

$\begin{aligned} x+(-1) \times 6=-4 \\ x=-4+6 \\ =+2 \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} CFSE & =-0.4\Delta_{0} \times 6+0.6\Delta_{0} \times 0 \\ & =-2.4\Delta_{0} \end{aligned}$

IV) $[Fe(CN)_{6}]^{3-}$

Oxidation state of $Fe:+3$

$Fe$ configuration $\rightarrow d^{6}s^{2}$

$Fe^{+3}$ configuration $\rightarrow d^{5}$

$\begin{aligned} x+6(-1)=-3 \\ x=-3+6 \\ =+3 \end{aligned}$

III) $[Fe(CN)_{6}]^{4-} \rightarrow -2.4\Delta_{0}$

IV) $[Fe((N)_{6}]^{3-} \rightarrow -2.0\Delta_{0}$

Stability of complexes based on $\Delta_{0}$ value, greater the CFSE value, more stable the complex.

The more negative the CFSE value, the move stable the complex.

So, complex with CFSE $-2.4\Delta$ is most stable and complex with CFSE $-1.6\Delta_{0}$ , is least stable. Stability order:

$\begin{aligned} & \begin{aligned} & -1.6\Delta_{0}<-1.8\Delta_{0}<-2.0\Delta_{0}<-2.4\Delta_{0} \\ & [Mn(CN)_{6}]^{3-}<[C(CN)_{6}]^{4-}<[Fe(CN)_{6}]^{3-}<[Fe(CN)_{6}]^{4-} \\ & I<II<IV<III \end{aligned} \\ & \text{Answer: Option (1)} \end{aligned}$

questions.explanation_text: The magnetic behavior of complexes can provide insights into their geometry and oxidation states. Given two complexes, $[NiCl_{4}]^{2-}$ and $[Ni(CO)_{4}]$ , we need to analyze the magnetic properties to deduce these characteristics. $[NiCl_{4}]^{2-}$ Oxidation State: In $[NiCl_{4}]^{2-}$ , nickel is in the +2 oxidation state ( $Ni^{2+}$ ). The electron configuration for $Ni^{2+}$ is $[Ar]3d^{8}4s^{0}$ . Geometry and Hybridization: The complex shows paramagnetic properties, indicating the presence of unpaired electrons. The hybridization in this case is $sp^{3}$ , which corresponds to a tetrahedral geometry. Thus, there are two unpaired electrons leading to its paramagnetism. $[Ni(CO)_{4}]$ Oxidation State: In this complex, nickel is in the zero oxidation state ( $Ni(0)$ ). The electron configuration is $[Ar]3d^{10}4s^{0}$ after rearrangement. Geometry and Hybridization: The compound is diamagnetic, indicating all electrons are paired. Its hybridization is also $sp^{3}$ , meaning the geometry is tetrahedral, resulting in no unpaired electrons and confirming its diamagnetic nature. In summary, $[NiCl_{4}]^{2-}$ is a tetrahedral complex with nickel in a +2 oxidation state and is paramagnetic. In contrast, $[Ni(CO)_{4}]$ is a tetrahedral complex with nickel in a 0 oxidation state and is diamagnetic.

questions.explanation_text: In octahedral complexes, which have a coordination number (CN) of 6, the formation of high spin or low spin complexes depends on the relative magnitude of the crystal field splitting energy, denoted as Δ₀, and the pairing energy (P.E.): If Δ₀ is less than the pairing energy (Δ₀ < P.E.), high spin complexes are formed. If Δ₀ is greater than the pairing energy (Δ₀ > P.E.), low spin complexes are formed. In tetrahedral complexes, where the coordination number is 4: The crystal field splitting energy (Δₜ) is typically less than the pairing energy (Δₜ < P.E.), resulting in the formation of mainly high spin complexes. Low spin complexes are rarely observed in tetrahedral coordination due to this energy consideration.

questions.question_text: The correct order of the following complexes in terms of their crystal field stabilization energies is :
questions.question_html: The correct order of the following complexes in terms of their crystal field stabilization energies is :
questions.explanation_text: The crystal field stabilization energy (CFSE) of a complex depends on two main factors: Charge/Oxidation State of the Central Metal Atom : Higher oxidation states generally lead to greater crystal field splitting energy (Δ). Field Strength of the Ligand : Stronger field ligands also result in greater splitting. Additionally, chelating ligands typically increase the field strength. For octahedral complexes, the CFSE is calculated as: $\text{CFSE}=[-0.4t_{2g}+0.6e_{g}]\Delta_{^{\circ}}$ Considering the complexes: $[\text{Co(en)}_{3}]^{3+}$ : Co exists as Co $^{3+}$ with electronic configuration $t_{2g}^{6}e_{g}^{0}$ . CFSE = $-2.4(\Delta_{0})_{1}$ . $[\text{Co(NH}_{3})_{6}]^{3+}$ : Co also as Co $^{3+}$ with $t_{2g}^{6}e_{g}^{0}$ . CFSE = $-2.4(\Delta_{0})_{2}$ . $[\text{Co(NH}_{3})_{6}]^{2+}$ : Co with Co $^{2+}$ configuration $t_{2g}^{5}e_{g}^{2}$ . CFSE = $-0.8(\Delta_{0})_{3}$ . $[\text{Co(NH}_{3})_{4}]^{2+}$ : Co as Co $^{2+}$ with different configuration $e^{4}t_{2}^{3}$ . CFSE = $-1.2\Delta_{t}$ , where $\Delta_{t}=\frac{4}{9}(\Delta_{0})_{3}$ . The order of crystal field splitting energies, based on our criteria, is: $\Delta_{t}<(\Delta_{0})_{3}<(\Delta_{0})_{2}<(\Delta_{0})_{1}$ Therefore, the CFSEs of these complexes compare as follows: $[\text{Co(en)}_{3}]^{3+}$ has the highest CFSE due to the $\Delta_{0}$ of the strongest field ligand and oxidation state. $[\text{Co(NH}_{3})_{6}]^{3+}$ follows with similarly high CFSE due to Co $^{3+}$ . $[\text{Co(NH}_{3})_{6}]^{2+}$ has a moderate CFSE. $[\text{Co(NH}_{3})_{4}]^{2+}$ has the lowest CFSE with $\Delta_{t}$ . This hierarchy of CFSE is determined by both the oxidation state of the cobalt metal and the field strength of the ligands involved.
questions.explanation_html:
The crystal field stabilization energy (CFSE) of a complex depends on two main factors:

Charge/Oxidation State of the Central Metal Atom: Higher oxidation states generally lead to greater crystal field splitting energy (Δ).

Field Strength of the Ligand: Stronger field ligands also result in greater splitting. Additionally, chelating ligands typically increase the field strength.

For octahedral complexes, the CFSE is calculated as:

$\text{CFSE}=[-0.4t_{2g}+0.6e_{g}]\Delta_{^{\circ}}$

Considering the complexes:

$[\text{Co(en)}_{3}]^{3+}$ :

Co exists as Co $^{3+}$ with electronic configuration $t_{2g}^{6}e_{g}^{0}$ .

CFSE = $-2.4(\Delta_{0})_{1}$ .

$[\text{Co(NH}_{3})_{6}]^{3+}$ :

Co also as Co $^{3+}$ with $t_{2g}^{6}e_{g}^{0}$ .

CFSE = $-2.4(\Delta_{0})_{2}$ .

$[\text{Co(NH}_{3})_{6}]^{2+}$ :

Co with Co $^{2+}$ configuration $t_{2g}^{5}e_{g}^{2}$ .

CFSE = $-0.8(\Delta_{0})_{3}$ .

$[\text{Co(NH}_{3})_{4}]^{2+}$ :

Co as Co $^{2+}$ with different configuration $e^{4}t_{2}^{3}$ .

CFSE = $-1.2\Delta_{t}$ , where $\Delta_{t}=\frac{4}{9}(\Delta_{0})_{3}$ .

The order of crystal field splitting energies, based on our criteria, is:

$\Delta_{t}<(\Delta_{0})_{3}<(\Delta_{0})_{2}<(\Delta_{0})_{1}$

Therefore, the CFSEs of these complexes compare as follows:

$[\text{Co(en)}_{3}]^{3+}$ has the highest CFSE due to the $\Delta_{0}$ of the strongest field ligand and oxidation state.

$[\text{Co(NH}_{3})_{6}]^{3+}$ follows with similarly high CFSE due to Co $^{3+}$ .

$[\text{Co(NH}_{3})_{6}]^{2+}$ has a moderate CFSE.

$[\text{Co(NH}_{3})_{4}]^{2+}$ has the lowest CFSE with $\Delta_{t}$ .

This hierarchy of CFSE is determined by both the oxidation state of the cobalt metal and the field strength of the ligands involved.

questions.question_html: The spin only magnetic moment ( $\mu$ ) value (B.M.) of the compound with strongest oxidising power among $Mn_{2}O_{3},TiO$ and VO is ____________ B.M. (Nearest integer).
questions.explanation_text: The compound with the strongest oxidizing power among Mn₂O₃, TiO, and VO is Mn₂O₃. This conclusion is based on the standard electrode potential ( $E^{\circ}$ ) value: $E_{\text{Mn}^{+3}/\text{Mn}^{+2}}^{\circ}=+1.57\text{V}$ For Mn³⁺, the electronic configuration is $d^{4}$ . The spin-only magnetic moment ( $\mu$ ) is calculated as follows: $\mu=\sqrt{n(n+2)}\text{BM}$ Where $n$ is the number of unpaired electrons. Here, $n=4$ : $\mu=\sqrt{4(4+2)}=\sqrt{24}\text{BM}$ This calculates to approximately 4.89 BM, which rounds to an integer value of 5 BM.

questions.question_text: The coordination environment of $Ca^{2+}$ ion in its complex with $EDTA^{4-}$ is :
questions.question_html: The coordination environment of $Ca^{2+}$ ion in its complex with $EDTA^{4-}$ is :
questions.explanation_text: The coordination environment of the $Ca^{2+}$ ion when it forms a complex with $EDTA^{4-}$ (ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid) is octahedral. Ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) is a hexadentate ligand, which means it has six donor atoms that can bind to a central metal ion. In the case of EDTA, these donor atoms are four oxygen atoms from its four carboxyl groups and two nitrogen atoms from its two amine groups. When $Ca^{2+}$ forms a complex with $EDTA^{4-}$ , all six donor atoms from EDTA coordinate with the calcium ion. As a result, the coordination number of the calcium ion is 6, leading to an octahedral geometry. This is because the octahedral geometry is the most common and energetically favorable arrangement for a coordination number of 6. In such a geometry, the six ligands are placed at equal distances from the central ion and at 90° angles relative to adjacent ligands, maximizing the distance between all ligands to minimize repulsion. The correct answer is Option B , octahedral.

questions.question_html: An octahedral complex with the formula $CoCl_{3} \cdot nNH_{3}$ upon reaction with excess of $AgNO_{3}$ solution gives 2 moles of $AgCl$ . Consider the oxidation state of $Co$ in the complex is ' $x$ '. The value of " $x+n$ " is __________.
questions.explanation_text: To solve this problem, we need to determine the oxidation state of cobalt ( $x$ ) and the number of ammonia molecules ( $n$ ) in the complex $CoCl_{3} \cdot nNH_{3}$ , given that it produces 2 moles of $AgCl$ upon reaction with excess $AgNO_{3}$ . First, let's write the reaction between the complex and $AgNO_{3}$ . The precipitate formation indicates that some chloride ions are free (not coordinated to the metal). Since 2 moles of $AgCl$ are formed, it indicates that there are 2 chloride ions that are free to react with $AgNO_{3}$ . Therefore, we can conclude that in the complex, 1 chloride ion is coordinated to the cobalt, and 2 chloride ions are free. This can be represented as: $[Co(NH_{3})_{n}Cl]Cl_{2}$ Now, let's determine the oxidation state of cobalt (Co). The charge on the entire complex should be zero, so we can write the charge balance equation as follows: The sum of the charges is: $x+(0 \cdot n)+(-1 \cdot 1)+(-1 \cdot 2)=0$ Solving this, we get: $x-1-2=0$ $x-3=0$ $x=3$ So, the oxidation state of Co is 3. Now, we need to find the value of $n$ . Since the coordination number of Co in an octahedral complex is typically 6 and we have 1 chloride ion coordinated to Co, the number of ammonia molecules coordinated to Co would be: $n=6-1=5$ Finally, we calculate $x+n$ : $x+n=3+5=8$ So, the value of " $x+n$ " is 8. Therefore, the correct option is: Option D: 8

First, let's write the reaction between the complex and $AgNO_{3}$ .

questions.question_html:
The number of complexes from the following with no electrons in the $t_{2}$ orbital is ______.

$TiCl_{4},[MnO_{4}]^{-},[FeO_{4}]^{2-},[FeCl_{4}]^{-},[CoCl_{4}]^{2-}$
questions.explanation_text: Identifying the electronic configuration and geometry : The condition "no electrons in the $t_{2}$ orbital" typically applies to a tetrahedral crystal field splitting pattern. In a tetrahedral field: The $d$ -orbitals split into two sets: $e$ (lower energy, 2 orbitals) and $t_{2}$ (higher energy, 3 orbitals). Electrons fill the lower-energy $e$ set before occupying the $t_{2}$ set. Thus, to have no electrons in $t_{2}$ , either: The metal has a $d^{0}$ configuration (no $d$ -electrons at all), or The $d$ -electron count is so low that all electrons can fit into the $e$ orbitals without needing to occupy $t_{2}$ . Analyzing each complex : (i) $TiCl_{4}$ : Ti in TiCl₄ is in the +4 oxidation state (since TiCl₄ is neutral and each Cl is -1). Ti (Z = 22) neutral : $3d^{2}4s^{2}$ . As Ti⁴⁺, it loses all 4 valence electrons (2 from 4s and 2 from 3d), resulting in $d^{0}$ . With $d^{0}$ , there are no electrons to occupy $t_{2}$ orbitals. No electrons in $t_{2}$ . (ii) $[MnO_{4}]^{-}$ (permanganate) : Mn in permanganate ( $MnO_{4}^{-}$ ) is in the +7 oxidation state. Mn (Z = 25) neutral is $3d^{5}4s^{2}$ . Mn⁷⁺ means removing all 7 valence electrons, leaving $d^{0}$ . With $d^{0}$ , no electrons in $t_{2}$ . No electrons in $t_{2}$ . (iii) $[FeO_{4}]^{2-}$ (ferrate) : Fe in $FeO_{4}^{2-}$ : Oxygen contributes -8 total. The ion is -2. Thus, Fe + (-8) = -2 → Fe = +6 oxidation state. Fe (Z = 26) neutral is $3d^{6}4s^{2}$ . Fe⁶⁺ means removing 6 electrons from the valence shell. After losing 2 from 4s and 4 from 3d, we get $d^{2}$ . In a tetrahedral field, $d^{2}$ fills the lower $e$ orbitals (2 electrons into e orbitals). No need to occupy $t_{2}$ orbitals since both electrons fit into e. No electrons in $t_{2}$ . (iv) $[FeCl_{4}]^{-}$ : Fe in $FeCl_{4}^{-}$ : Cl total charge = -4, complex = -1, so Fe = +3. Fe(III) is $d^{5}$ . In a tetrahedral field, with 5 $d$ -electrons, after filling the 2 $e$ orbitals, we have 3 more electrons that must go into $t_{2}$ . Has electrons in $t_{2}$ . (v) $[CoCl_{4}]^{2-}$ : Co in $CoCl_{4}^{2-}$ : Cl total = -4, complex = -2, so Co = +2. Co(II) is $d^{7}$ . For $d^{7}$ , even after filling the $e$ set (2 orbitals), we have 5 more electrons left, which must occupy the $t_{2}$ orbitals. Has electrons in $t_{2}$ . Counting the complexes with no electrons in $t_{2}$ : TiCl₄: No electrons in $t_{2}$ . [MnO₄]⁻: No electrons in $t_{2}$ . [FeO₄]²⁻: No electrons in $t_{2}$ . [FeCl₄]⁻: Has electrons in $t_{2}$ . [CoCl₄]²⁻: Has electrons in $t_{2}$ . Total with no electrons in $t_{2}$ = 3. Answer : 3
questions.explanation_html:
Identifying the electronic configuration and geometry :

The condition "no electrons in the $t_{2}$ orbital" typically applies to a tetrahedral crystal field splitting pattern. In a tetrahedral field:

The $d$ -orbitals split into two sets: $e$ (lower energy, 2 orbitals) and $t_{2}$ (higher energy, 3 orbitals).

Electrons fill the lower-energy $e$ set before occupying the $t_{2}$ set.

Thus, to have no electrons in $t_{2}$ , either:

The metal has a $d^{0}$ configuration (no $d$ -electrons at all), or

The $d$ -electron count is so low that all electrons can fit into the $e$ orbitals without needing to occupy $t_{2}$ .

Analyzing each complex :

(i) $TiCl_{4}$ :

Ti in TiCl₄ is in the +4 oxidation state (since TiCl₄ is neutral and each Cl is -1).

Ti (Z = 22) neutral : $3d^{2}4s^{2}$ . As Ti⁴⁺, it loses all 4 valence electrons (2 from 4s and 2 from 3d), resulting in $d^{0}$ .

With $d^{0}$ , there are no electrons to occupy $t_{2}$ orbitals.

No electrons in $t_{2}$ .

(ii) $[MnO_{4}]^{-}$ (permanganate) :

Mn in permanganate ( $MnO_{4}^{-}$ ) is in the +7 oxidation state.

Mn (Z = 25) neutral is $3d^{5}4s^{2}$ . Mn⁷⁺ means removing all 7 valence electrons, leaving $d^{0}$ .

With $d^{0}$ , no electrons in $t_{2}$ .

No electrons in $t_{2}$ .

(iii) $[FeO_{4}]^{2-}$ (ferrate) :

Fe in $FeO_{4}^{2-}$ : Oxygen contributes -8 total. The ion is -2. Thus, Fe + (-8) = -2 → Fe = +6 oxidation state.

Fe (Z = 26) neutral is $3d^{6}4s^{2}$ . Fe⁶⁺ means removing 6 electrons from the valence shell. After losing 2 from 4s and 4 from 3d, we get $d^{2}$ .

In a tetrahedral field, $d^{2}$ fills the lower $e$ orbitals (2 electrons into e orbitals).

No need to occupy $t_{2}$ orbitals since both electrons fit into e.

No electrons in $t_{2}$ .

(iv) $[FeCl_{4}]^{-}$ :

Fe in $FeCl_{4}^{-}$ : Cl total charge = -4, complex = -1, so Fe = +3.

Fe(III) is $d^{5}$ .

In a tetrahedral field, with 5 $d$ -electrons, after filling the 2 $e$ orbitals, we have 3 more electrons that must go into $t_{2}$ .

Has electrons in $t_{2}$ .

(v) $[CoCl_{4}]^{2-}$ :

Co in $CoCl_{4}^{2-}$ : Cl total = -4, complex = -2, so Co = +2.

Co(II) is $d^{7}$ .

For $d^{7}$ , even after filling the $e$ set (2 orbitals), we have 5 more electrons left, which must occupy the $t_{2}$ orbitals.

Has electrons in $t_{2}$ .

Counting the complexes with no electrons in $t_{2}$ :

TiCl₄: No electrons in $t_{2}$ .

[MnO₄]⁻: No electrons in $t_{2}$ .

[FeO₄]²⁻: No electrons in $t_{2}$ .

[FeCl₄]⁻: Has electrons in $t_{2}$ .

[CoCl₄]²⁻: Has electrons in $t_{2}$ .

Total with no electrons in $t_{2}$ = 3.

Answer :

questions.explanation_text: A homoleptic complex is one in which a central metal atom or ion is surrounded by only one kind of donor groups, ligands or ions. On the other hand, a heteroleptic complex contains a central metal surrounded by more than one kind of donor groups, ligands or ions. Let's examine the given options : Option A: $[Ni(NH_{3})_{2}Cl_{2}]$ This complex contains two different ligands, ammonia ( $NH_{3}$ ) and chloride (Cl). Therefore, it is a heteroleptic complex. Option B: $[Co(NH_{3})_{4}Cl_{2}]^{+}$ Just like Option A, this complex has two types of ligands, ammonia ( $NH_{3}$ ) and chloride (Cl), making it a heteroleptic complex. Option C: $[Fe(NH_{3})_{4}Cl_{2}]^{+}$ Again, this complex has ammonia ( $NH_{3}$ ) and chloride (Cl) ligands, so it is a heteroleptic complex. Option D: $[Ni(CN)_{4}]^{2-}$ This complex has only cyanide (CN) ligands surrounding the nickel ion, with no other types of ligands present. Thus, this is a homoleptic complex because it is coordinated by a single type of ligand. Therefore, Option D is the correct answer as it represents a homoleptic complex.

questions.question_text: The number of unpaired d-electrons in $[Co(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{3+}$ is ________.
questions.question_html: The number of unpaired d-electrons in $[Co(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{3+}$ is ________.
questions.explanation_text: First, let us determine the $d$ -electron count of the cobalt center in $[Co(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{3+}$ . 1. Oxidation state and $d$ -electron count Neutral cobalt (Co) has an atomic number of 27 and an electronic configuration: $Co[Ar]3d^{7}4s^{2}.$ In the +3 oxidation state , cobalt has lost a total of 3 electrons: First two electrons are removed from the $4s$ orbital. The third electron is removed from the $3d$ orbitals. Thus, $Co^{3+}$ has $3d^{7-1}=3d^{6}.$ So in $[Co(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{3+}$ , the cobalt center is $d^{6}$ . 2. High-spin vs Low-spin for $Co^{3+}$ Even though $H_{2}O$ is generally considered a weak field ligand, the $Co^{3+}$ ion has a relatively high charge (+3). A higher charge on the metal center usually increases the ligand-field splitting ( $\Delta_{o}$ ) significantly compared to lower oxidation states of the same metal. In most typical octahedral complexes of $Co^{3+}$ , the splitting $\Delta_{o}$ is large enough that the complex ends up being low spin . Electronic configuration in an octahedral field For a $d^{6}$ octahedral low-spin complex, all six electrons pair up in the lower-energy $t_{2g}$ orbitals: $t_{2g}^{6}e_{g}^{0}$ That leaves 0 unpaired electrons. 3. Final answer Therefore, the number of unpaired $d$ -electrons in $[Co(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{3+}$ is $0.$ Correct Option: A (0)
questions.explanation_html:
First, let us determine the $d$ -electron count of the cobalt center in $[Co(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{3+}$ .

1. Oxidation state and $d$ -electron count

Neutral cobalt (Co) has an atomic number of 27 and an electronic configuration:

$Co[Ar]3d^{7}4s^{2}.$

In the +3 oxidation state, cobalt has lost a total of 3 electrons:

First two electrons are removed from the $4s$ orbital.

The third electron is removed from the $3d$ orbitals.

Thus, $Co^{3+}$ has

$3d^{7-1}=3d^{6}.$

So in $[Co(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{3+}$ , the cobalt center is $d^{6}$ .

2. High-spin vs Low-spin for $Co^{3+}$

Even though $H_{2}O$ is generally considered a weak field ligand, the $Co^{3+}$ ion has a relatively high charge (+3). A higher charge on the metal center usually increases the ligand-field splitting ( $\Delta_{o}$ ) significantly compared to lower oxidation states of the same metal.

In most typical octahedral complexes of $Co^{3+}$ , the splitting $\Delta_{o}$ is large enough that the complex ends up being low spin.

Electronic configuration in an octahedral field

For a $d^{6}$ octahedral low-spin complex, all six electrons pair up in the lower-energy $t_{2g}$ orbitals:

$t_{2g}^{6}e_{g}^{0}$

That leaves 0 unpaired electrons.

3. Final answer

Therefore, the number of unpaired $d$ -electrons in

$[Co(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{3+}$ is $0.$

Correct Option: A (0)

However, $Mn$ has a complex crystal structure leading to a metallic radius that is anomalously high compared to its neighbors. The actual values (in pm) are approximately: $Sc$ : 164 $Ti$ : 147 $V$ : 135 $Cr$ : 129 $Mn$ : 137 (anomalously high) $Zn$ : 137 (larger due to full d-subshell shielding) Among the options provided ( $Sc,Ti,V,Cr,Mn,Zn$ ), Chromium ( $Cr$ ) has the smallest metallic radius. Therefore, $M=Cr$ . Step 2: Determine the oxidation state of Cr in the complex. The complex is $CrO_{4}^{2-}$ (Chromate ion). Let the oxidation state of $Cr$ be $x$ . The oxidation state of Oxygen ( $O$ ) is generally $-2$ . The sum of oxidation states equals the charge on the ion: $x+4(-2)=-2$ $x-8=-2$ $x=+6$ So, Chromium is in the $+6$ oxidation state ( $Cr^{6+}$ ). Step 3: Determine the electronic configuration. The atomic number of Chromium ( $Cr$ ) is 24. Ground state configuration of $Cr$ : $[Ar]3d^{5}4s^{1}$ To form $Cr^{6+}$ , we remove the outer 6 electrons (one from $4s$ and five from $3d$ ).
